title: Passover: Elijah's cup
hookLine: a cup is poured for Elijah and the door is opened

cards: It's late. The meal is over, grace after meals is said, and the children are fading. Then someone fills a large, often beautiful cup that's sat untouched all night.
A child is sent to open the front door, and cold air comes in. Everyone stands, or goes quiet, or sings.
The youngest kids watch the cup closely, certain that if they look hard enough, they'll see the wine go down a little. Nobody invited this guest. He's been expected for a very long time.

teach.b: The guest is Elijah, the prophet. In the book of Kings, the text never says he dies; he's carried up to heaven in a whirlwind, with a chariot of fire. So in Jewish tradition, he never quite left.
He turns up in Talmudic stories disguised as a traveler, a beggar, a merchant. And Malachi, whose book closes the Prophets, ends with a promise: God will send Elijah before the great day of the LORD.
In the old Jewish translation: "And he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers." So Elijah became the messenger of redemption. Why a cup?
Are there four cups at the seder, or five? Some versions of the Talmud mention a fifth.

A popular later explanation says that since the question was never settled, a fifth cup is poured, not drunk, and named for Elijah, who, tradition says, will one day answer the questions the rabbis left open.
Why open the door? It's opened right before a passage asking God to pour out wrath on the nations that devoured Israel, words from the Psalms, said in years of real persecution.
The Torah calls this night a night of watching, so some explain there's nothing to fear in opening the door. And Elijah, if he's coming, should find it open.
More recently, some families add a cup of water for Miriam, the prophet, beside Elijah's; others keep the older custom alone.
Either way, the seder ends with the door open, waiting.

how: Near the end of the seder, after grace after meals, families fill a cup for Elijah and open the front door while reciting 'Pour out Your wrath' from the Psalms; some families now also place a cup of water for Miriam.

a winter festival of lights and of rededication

games.q: the rabbis can't decide whether the seder has four cups or five. the question was never settled. what does the tradition do?
o: drink four, and leave it there.
pour a fifth, name it for Elijah, and don't drink it.
games.why: a fifth cup is poured for Elijah, who, tradition says, will one day answer the questions the rabbis left open.

practice: If you can, open a door or a window and feel the air change. Think of what you're waiting for: a reconciliation, a recovery, a turn in the world, a guest you haven't met yet.
Malachi's promise was about hearts turning toward each other, so stay with one heart you'd like turned toward you, or yours toward them.

wordCard.voice: Passover. The festival of leaving Egypt, and a night that ends with Elijah's cup poured and the door left open. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: leave the door open. In Jewish tradition, Elijah is still expected. Day six hundred eighty-two, done.
